name: Push Press
description: The push press is a compound overhead pressing exercise that uses a brief, explosive leg drive (dip and drive) to initiate the press, allowing more weight to be lifted overhead than a strict overhead press. The legs provide initial momentum through the sticking point, after which the shoulders and triceps complete the press to lockout. It is a staple movement in Olympic weightlifting training and functional strength programs.

execution.starting_position: Hold the barbell in a front rack position at the front deltoids, just above the clavicle. Feet are shoulder-width apart, slightly outside hip-width. Elbows are slightly in front of the bar.
execution.setup_instructions: Set the bar in a rack at shoulder height. Clean or take the bar from the rack to the front rack position. Ensure adequate overhead clearance.
steps: Step 1: Hold the bar in the front rack position, elbows slightly forward. Feet shoulder-width apart.
Step 2: Dip slightly at the knees and hips — a shallow, quick bend of approximately 10–15 degrees.
Step 3: Explosively reverse the dip with leg drive, extending hips and knees rapidly to generate upward momentum.
Step 4: Use the momentum to press the bar overhead to full lockout, finishing with ears in front of the arms overhead.
execution.breathing_instructions: Inhale and brace before the dip; exhale at the top of the press.
common_mistakes: Dipping too deep, turning it into a squat and losing the rapid leg drive timing
Pressing forward rather than straight up — the bar should travel vertically
safety_considerations: Learn the strict overhead press first to establish the pressing path before adding leg drive
Use a rack to get the bar into position safely at heavy loads
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full lockout overhead with the bar over the mid-foot; full return to the front rack position.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Explosive drive then controlled descent — no tempo count
coaching_cues: Dip straight down, drive straight up — no forward lean
The dip is quick and shallow — a calf raise, not a squat
